strengths: Novel research question bridging cognitive science and AI: investigates whether LLMs exhibit human-like biases toward semantic efficiency without explicit training
Sound theoretical framework: principled application of Information Bottleneck principle to understand semantic categorization
Creative methodology: IICLL paradigm cleverly adapts iterated language learning to test inductive biases beyond training data
Clear presentation: well-written paper with effective visualizations that communicate experimental design and results
Consistent empirical findings: robust convergence toward IB-efficiency across multiple metrics, generations, and initializations
Systematic comparison: tests multiple models (Gemini, Llama), input modalities (text, image), and provides good visualization of convergence trajectories
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: only one semantic domain (color) and two models; claims about "LLMs" in general are not supported; generalizability to other semantic categories unclear
Incomplete manuscript: missing citation '[?]' on page 2 indicates paper not fully prepared, raising quality concerns
Insufficient analysis of model differences: Llama shows systematically lower complexity than English, but explanations are speculative; differences undermine claims of universal IB bias
Unclear causal mechanism: paper shows convergence to IB-efficiency but doesn't prove this reflects an inductive bias versus other mechanisms like implicit pressure from next-token prediction training
Training data leakage inadequately addressed: Gemini's English alignment could reflect memorized patterns; pseudowords processed by models trained on billions of natural language examples
Missing methodological details: exact prompts, hyperparameters, and metric computation not specified; no ablations on sample size, categories, or initialization; significantly limits reproducibility
Weak baselines: no comparison with non-LLM systems or smaller models; unclear how much convergence is LLM-specific versus general to the IICLL process
Overstated claims: abstract and title use causal language ('reflect a learning bias') and broad generalization not warranted by single-domain evidence
Statistical analysis incomplete: no significance testing despite claims of robustness; source of randomness in 'random seeds' unclear
Generalization concerns: color naming is unique (continuous perceptual space, high cross-linguistic availability); findings may not extend to more abstract semantic categories

strengths: Well-motivated research question connecting cognitive science and AI: examining whether LLMs spontaneously develop human-aligned semantic systems without explicit training for IB-efficiency
Theoretically grounded framework using Information Bottleneck theory, which has strong empirical support across human languages
Complementary experimental design: direct color naming combined with iterated language learning provides both alignment evidence and inductive bias evidence
Clear presentation of results with informative visualizations showing efficiency-accuracy tradeoffs and convergence trajectories
Reasonable experimental rigor with results averaged over 10 random seeds and reported uncertainty
weaknesses: Severely limited model diversity: only two models tested (Gemini 2.0-flash, Llama 3.3-70B). Since in-context capabilities vary, these findings may not generalize. A top-tier venue would expect demonstration across a broader model family

Critical ambiguity in distinguishing inductive bias from training data effects: LLMs have been extensively trained on color naming and color category discussions across languages and WCS data. The IICLL paradigm with pseudowords doesn't adequately isolate whether convergence to IB-efficiency reflects genuine inductive biases or compressed training patterns

Insufficient mechanistic insight: the paper demonstrates convergence to efficiency but provides no analysis of *why*. Could this reflect (a) memorized compression patterns from training data, (b) general compression principles in deep learning, or (c) properties of color space itself? These alternatives are unaddressed

Incomplete/missing methodological details: (1) crucial citation showing '[?]' indicating incomplete references, (2) prompt construction not provided, (3) definition of 'pseudowords' unclear, (4) number of generations for IICLL not stated, (5) how the counterfactual baseline is computed not explained

Input modality confound inadequately addressed: Gemini-img vs Gemini-txt show substantially different behavior (text more efficient, images more human-aligned). This suggests results are sensitive to implementation details rather than reflecting fundamental principles, yet receives minimal analysis

Model size as confound: Llama's lower complexity is attributed to model size, but this is speculation without investigation. Systematic ablation with different model sizes would be needed to establish this

Incomplete IICLL validation: the human IL experiments involved actual social learning dynamics across people. LLM IICLL is a single model iterating—the parallel may not hold. No analysis of how this differs from human transmission

Limited evaluation metrics: only efficiency loss, IB-alignment, and human-alignment examined. Missing: (1) analysis of which specific color categories each model develops, (2) error analysis examining where LLMs diverge from humans, (3) statistical significance testing beyond standard deviations, (4) ablation studies

Overclaimed conclusions: (1) 'perceptually grounded' is misleading—LLMs don't perceive colors, (2) 'driven by the same fundamental principle' is not established—convergence could be coincidental or reflect compressed training data, (3) claims about inductive bias exceed what the experiments demonstrate

Narrow scope limiting generalizability: only color naming examined. While acknowledged, this severely constrains conclusions about LLM inductive biases more broadly. Single-domain findings don't support broad claims about semantic system evolution
Human-alignment metric under-specified: how is 'structural similarity' computed? The paper doesn't provide sufficient detail to understand or reproduce this critical evaluation measure

Training data concerns not adequately addressed: no discussion of whether LLMs may have encountered WCS data or color naming studies in training, or how one would disentangle memorization from learned principles
Unclear efficiency loss computation: how is the IB objective (Eq. 1) evaluated for LLM outputs? Which β value? How is the IB bound determined when evaluating LLMs? These details are crucial but vague

Weak novelty for AI venue: the IB framework is from Zaslavsky et al. (2018), the ILL paradigm from Xu et al. (2022), and the human-LLM comparison from prior work. Main contribution is applying IICLL to LLMs—relatively incremental for a top-tier AI conference

strengths: Novel and well-motivated research question connecting cognitive science and LLMs with clear relevance to understanding LLM alignment
Strong theoretical framework using Information Bottleneck principle with established grounding in cognitive science literature
Innovative IICLL methodology that cleverly adapts iterated language learning to probe implicit inductive biases beyond training data
Clear experimental design with two complementary studies (English color naming and IICLL convergence) that address different aspects of the research question
Comprehensive evaluation using multiple metrics (efficiency loss, IB-alignment, human-alignment) with clear visualizations of results
Interesting analysis of input modality effects (text vs. image) showing how representations influence model behavior
Well-written presentation with effective figures that communicate the theoretical framework and empirical results
weaknesses: Critical missing citations: Multiple '[? ]' placeholders in Section 3.2 appear to reference foundational prior work but are incomplete, suggesting insufficient manuscript preparation and hindering reproducibility
Severely limited generalizability: Evaluation restricted to single semantic domain (color naming); claims about LLMs evolving 'human-like semantic systems' are overgeneralized from narrow evidence
Very limited model coverage: Only two models tested; both are recent, high-capability models; most open-weights models cannot perform IICLL, limiting claims about 'LLMs' generally

Overclaimed 'perceptual grounding': LLMs lack embodied perception equivalent to humans; Gemini's image processing is qualitatively different from human sensorimotor grounding and this distinction should be clearly stated

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: Paper does not explain why efficiency bias emerges—is it inherent to language modeling, specific training procedures, or architectural choices? Speculation about input modality is underdeveloped
Incomplete robustness reporting: Claims that results were 'replicated with added input noise' but provides no results, methods, or analysis of these critical robustness checks
Underspecified IICLL implementation: Missing key details on number of color-pseudoword pairs per generation, number of generations, pseudoword generation procedure, and exact prompts used

Undefined 'counterfactual baseline': Figure 1H references a 'strong counterfactual baseline' but text never defines what these hypothetical variants are or how they were computed, limiting interpretability of key results

Limited analysis of model differences: Why does Llama consistently produce lower complexity? Why does Gemini-txt outperform Gemini-img on efficiency but not human-alignment? These patterns deserve systematic investigation

Insufficient human comparison: IICLL comparison relies on single human study [22]; more discussion of human variability and whether LLM patterns truly replicate human patterns would strengthen central claims

Training data contamination concern: While IICLL uses random initializations, cannot fully rule out that convergence patterns reflect memorized linguistic associations rather than genuine inductive biases

Unclear IB computation: How are mental representations operationalized from LLM outputs? How are I(M;W) and I(W;U) computed? Is Gaussian noise model appropriate for systems without human-like perception?
Limited ablation studies: No systematic investigation of model size, architecture, or training procedure effects; only input modality variations explored
WCS dataset limitations not addressed: Non-industrialized society focus may introduce cultural/economic biases; impact on comparisons not discussed

strengths: Novel IICLL methodology that enables direct comparison with human iterated learning experiments
Comprehensive evaluation of 39 LLMs across 6 families with systematic variation in size and training approach
Well-motivated research question with appropriate domain choice (color naming provides rich human data)
Clear empirical findings showing instruction-tuned models achieve better English alignment and Gemini 2.0 develops human-like IB-efficient systems
Rigorous evaluation framework grounded in Information Bottleneck theory with multiple validation approaches (efficiency metrics, NID alignment, rotation analysis)
High-quality presentation with excellent visualizations and extensive appendices supporting reproducibility
Strong reproducibility provisions including model identification, example prompts, and code commitment
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: nearly 95% of results are about color naming; Shepard circles experiment is preliminary (qualitative only, single model tested, no rigorous evaluation), undermining claims about general principles

Critical mechanistic questions remain unanswered: Why do LLMs evolve toward IB efficiency? Is it training data properties, instruction-tuning, model scale, or general inductive biases? This gap substantially limits the contribution's significance
Results overwhelmingly dependent on Gemini 2.0; other state-of-the-art models (Gemma, Llama, Qwen) show much weaker performance; no analysis of what distinguishes Gemini 2.0
Model collapse to single-word systems in smaller models (Appendix L) is buried in appendix despite being central to understanding necessary capabilities; should be prominent in main text

IICLL experimental design choices inadequately justified: sliding window history (10 interactions) differs from human experiments without sensitivity analysis; 6× vocabulary sampling choice unexplored; constrained vocabulary differs from human experiments
Selection bias: only models performing well on English naming tested in main IICLL; weaker models relegated to appendix; limits understanding of which capabilities enable efficiency

Brittleness to input format: performance severely degrades with CIELAB coordinates (Appendix C); described as testing 'ideal conditions' but suggests results may not reflect robust semantic understanding
Limited statistical testing: most comparisons rely on visual inspection and confidence intervals; formal significance tests largely absent
Most models fail at English color naming; observation that some produce WCS-like rather than English-like systems not investigated; incomplete analysis of failure modes

Heavy dependence on in-context learning capacity for IICLL results; unclear whether findings reflect semantic efficiency preferences or in-context learning ability; limited ablation distinguishing these factors

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical framework connecting Information Bottleneck theory, cognitive science, and LLM behavior through color naming provides compelling intellectual grounding
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 39 models with systematic variations in size, instruction-tuning, and modality; extensive ablations and appendices demonstrate thoroughness
Novel IICLL methodology creatively extends I-ICL to simulate cultural transmission; rotation analysis cleverly verifies that evolved systems are non-arbitrary
Strong reproducibility practices including detailed prompts, complete model lists, hyperparameter justifications, and commitment to release code
Multiple rigorous evaluation metrics (efficiency loss, IB-alignment, WCS-alignment, NID) provide comprehensive assessment from different theoretical angles
Principled comparison to human iterated learning data (Xu et al. 2013) provides meaningful behavioral baseline
Analysis of training dynamics (OLMo checkpoints, Appendix F) reveals interesting emergence of alignment with instruction-tuning
weaknesses: Central claim about 'inductive biases toward IB-efficiency' is overstated relative to evidence: showing convergence under IICLL does not definitively demonstrate an inductive bias, and the paper acknowledges uncertainty about origins of this property

Severe generalization limitations: only Gemini 2.0 achieves human-like range of IB-tradeoffs; other models converge to fundamentally different low-complexity solutions. Paper provides no mechanistic explanation for why Gemini differs

Limited to single domain (color naming) despite generalization claims; Shepard circles analysis (Section 4.3) is preliminary, qualitative, and only tests Gemini—insufficient to support domain-generality claims

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: paper documents what happens but cannot explain why—is this memorization of training patterns, effect of instruction-tuning, or emergent in-context learning property? This gap is fundamental for a paper claiming to demonstrate inductive biases
IICLL procedure concerns: 10-item context window is justified post-hoc; procedure differs mechanistically from human learning; k=14 condition only Gemini succeeds, creating unequal model comparison

Models fail dramatically with CIELAB color encoding (Appendix C) but paper sidesteps this by using sRGB in main experiments, raising questions about whether models learned robust perceptual representations or merely memorized sRGB patterns

Core novelty is limited: finding that larger instruction-tuned models outperform smaller/base models is unsurprising and well-established; application of IB theory is interesting but primarily reformulates existing findings

Unexplained discrepancies with prior work: Marjieh et al. (2024) reported several models recover English color naming, but many models here fail; paper does not clearly explain whether this reflects different methods or genuine differences

Limited statistical rigor: minimal formal significance testing despite 39 models and numerous comparisons; multiple comparison corrections not addressed; baseline comparisons limited to single nearest-neighbor baseline

Shepard circles section underdeveloped: only Gemini tested, only qualitative description, no quantitative metrics, no human baseline comparison—inclusion undermines generality claims without sufficient analysis

Claims in abstract and introduction substantially overstate conclusions (e.g., 'same fundamental principle that underlies human languages') relative to evidence limited to Gemini on one domain with unclear mechanism

strengths: Novel IICLL methodology that cleverly adapts iterated learning for LLMs, enabling direct comparison with human cognitive experiments
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 39 models with systematic variation of size, instruction-tuning, and modality
Strong theoretical grounding in Information Bottleneck principle and iterated learning theory from cognitive science
Convincing quantitative evidence that LLMs develop IB-efficient systems, with Gemini 2.0 uniquely capturing human-like complexity range
Excellent reproducibility: detailed appendices with prompts, model IDs, procedures, and planned code release
Clever rotation analysis demonstrating that efficiency is constrained by perceptual structure rather than arbitrary
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and logical flow connecting cognitive science to modern AI
weaknesses: Limited domain generalization: color has exceptional properties (rich online data, perceptual grounding, universal patterns); Shepard circles analysis is preliminary (Gemini only); generalization claims are speculative

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: paper identifies that IB-efficiency emerges but not why; discussion of origins (training data, instruction-tuning, scale) is superficial; no ablations isolating causal factors
In-context learning capacity as confound: unclear whether observed differences reflect genuine inductive bias versus simply weak in-context learning ability in smaller models
IICLL design choices need better justification: sliding window of 10 interactions is non-standard; different initialization from Xu et al.; sRGB representation choice not human-inspired
Sensitivity to representation format: CIELAB inputs cause performance degradation (Appendix C); results appear highly dependent on sRGB encoding, limiting generalization
Statistical rigor gaps: no formal significance testing for key claims; confidence intervals inconsistently reported; comparisons lack formal support
English color naming inconsistencies unexplained: many state-of-the-art models fail to recover English; some produce WCS-like systems instead—raises robustness concerns
Communication pressure missing from IICLL: human color terms evolved under both transmission and communication; acknowledged as limitation but not adequately addressed

No explanation for why Gemini is unique: paper documents that Gemini 2.0 uniquely captures complexity range but provides no analysis of the underlying cause (architecture, training, scale, in-context learning)
